items.stem: A team preparing to launch an assistant sets its content-safety target as a hard 0% policy-violation rate, graded by a model classifier over a rolling window of 10,000 conversations, ahead of trust-and-safety sign-off. What threshold should the team set?

opts.t: Keep the target at a literal 0% policy-violation rate and treat any single violation as a launch-blocking failure.
Enforce the 0% target with a deterministic pattern check against the model's raw output text.
Drop the numeric threshold and have the trust-and-safety lead review flagged conversations weekly instead.
Re-anchor the bar to a small achievable non-zero rate, such as under 0.1% of the sampled window.

items.whyRight: An open-ended, model-graded property cannot sustain a hard zero — one miss makes the bar non-binding and future violations go unflagged. Re-anchoring to a small, deliberately achievable non-zero rate, set before results are seen, keeps the threshold a real gate rather than an aspiration nobody enforces.

whyWrong.A: A literal 0% target on an open-ended, model-judged property becomes non-binding the first time any violation occurs, since the bar cannot be sustained.
whyWrong.B: The property is model-graded, not deterministic; no pattern or field scan can decide whether free-text output is policy-violating.
whyWrong.C: Removing the numeric threshold entirely leaves no gate at all, and weekly qualitative review cannot substitute for a measured, agreed-in-advance rate.

items.t1Clause: graded by a model classifier — invert to a deterministic exact-match scan for a specific forbidden token, making the property code-checkable
items.factAnswerRaw: Re-anchor to a small non-zero rate (e.g. < 0.1% of 10,000)

items.stem: A RAG assistant's single overall quality metric drops twelve points, and the team must isolate which layer caused it before the release manager will approve the next deploy. Applying the two-layer evaluation principle, what should the team do?

opts.t: Refine the rubric used to compute the single overall quality score.
Move the pipeline to a higher-capability generation model to raise the overall score.
Read the retrieval and generation bars already tracked separately, and treat retrieval as the likely fault.
Split the score into a retrieval row (Recall@k) and a generation row (faithfulness), each cleared against its own bar.

items.whyRight: A blended score cannot say which layer moved. Splitting into a retrieval row measured against gold passage ids and a generation row measured for faithfulness isolates the regression to the layer that actually failed, since each layer must clear its own bar independently.

whyWrong.A: A better rubric still scores one blended number, so it still cannot attribute a regression to retrieval or to generation specifically.
whyWrong.B: A higher-capability model was never shown to be at fault, and it can produce more fluent answers over the same broken passages.
whyWrong.C: The stem states there is only a single blended score; separate retrieval and generation bars do not yet exist to read.

items.t1Clause: one overall quality metric, regression cannot be located — invert to the retrieval and generation bars already being tracked separately at 0.55 and 0.97
items.factAnswerRaw: Split into retrieval and generation rows

items.stem: A support assistant's accuracy drops the same week a prompt change ships to production handling 50,000 tickets weekly. Investigation shows the drop correlates with a simultaneous data-schema change, not the prompt. What should the team do before the on-call lead signs off?

opts.t: Roll back the prompt change immediately and monitor the quality dashboard for further drops.
Run the regression set and a controlled A/B against the prompt change, since it shipped right before the drop.
Re-run the regression set and a controlled A/B investigation against the data-schema change rather than the prompt edit.
Escalate to a higher-capability model, since the current model may no longer handle the task reliably.

items.whyRight: The timing coincidence points at the prompt, but the stated evidence points at the data-schema change instead. Attribution requires isolating the actual variable that moved, so the regression set and a controlled A/B must be re-run against the schema change, not the unrelated prompt edit.

whyWrong.A: Rolling back the prompt does nothing if the schema change is the actual cause, and dashboard monitoring only catches damage after users absorb it.
whyWrong.B: The stem already states the drop correlates with the schema change, not the prompt; testing the prompt again investigates a variable the evidence already clears.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the evidence implicates the model itself, and a bigger model would not fix answers built on a broken upstream schema.

items.t1Clause: correlates with a simultaneous data-schema change, not the prompt — invert so the drop instead correlates specifically with the prompt change, with no schema change involved
items.factAnswerRaw: Re-run the regression set and a controlled A/B investigation against the data-schema change rather than the prompt edit.

items.stem: An agent handles single-step lookups correctly but fails broadly on tasks needing three or more reasoning steps. Retrieval Recall@k is verified at 0.94 and the prompt has passed clean review. What does this pattern indicate before the team funds further prompt rewrites?

opts.t: Retrieval is still the likely fault, so Recall@k should be re-measured before any other conclusion is drawn.
The prompt still contains ambiguous wording and needs a further rewrite, despite passing review.
Model mismatch: the model's reasoning capability is insufficient for this task, since every upstream layer is already cleared.
The application is failing to resend conversation history, causing context loss across turns.

items.whyRight: Retrieval and prompt are the cheaper, earlier layers and both have already cleared, which is precisely the signature the diagnosis order reserves for model mismatch: a broad failure on genuinely multi-step reasoning after every upstream layer is confirmed clean.

whyWrong.A: The stem already states Recall@k is verified at 0.94, so retrieval has already cleared and cannot be the fault.
whyWrong.B: The prompt already passed clean review; another rewrite patches a layer that was never implicated in the failure.
whyWrong.D: Lost conversation history explains forgotten facts across turns, not a broad multi-step reasoning failure verified against clean retrieval and prompt.

items.t1Clause: Retrieval Recall@k is verified at 0.94 — invert to Recall@k measured low (e.g. 0.55), leaving retrieval unverified

items.stem: A regulated support system sends an identical, compliance-mandated preamble on every request. Both p95 latency and monthly token cost exceed target, and the platform lead must approve the fix before next quarter's budget review. Select the two appropriate actions.

opts.t: Cut the preamble by 60% to only the sections used most often.
Reorder the prompt so the static preamble comes first and enable prompt caching.
Add a model call at request time to summarize the preamble before sending it.
Decline the proposal to cut the preamble, since the removed sections are compliance-mandated.

items.whyRight: Reordering for a stable prefix and enabling caching reuses the same required content at a fraction of the cost and latency, while declining the cut preserves compliance-mandated sections a proposed 60% reduction would remove — both actions preserve everything the requirement demands.

whyWrong.A: Cutting the preamble removes compliance-mandated content to solve a problem caching solves without losing anything, and none of it may legally be dropped.
whyWrong.C: An extra model call sounds like a sophisticated compression step, but it adds its own full invocation cost and latency and degrades policy precision.

items.t1Clause: the preamble is compliance-mandated — invert so the removed sections are unrequired boilerplate rather than compliance content
items.factAnswerRaw: Order static content first and enable prompt caching; Reject if the removed sections are required
